chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Fadalah from Husayn ibn 'Uthman from Ibn Muskān from Abū Bakr al-Ḍaḥrāmī said:

I asked Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who prays while henna is on him. He said: 'He does not pray while it is on him, but he removes it if he intends to pray.' I said: 'His henna and the cloth covering it are clean.' He said: 'He does not pray while it is on him, and the woman likewise does not pray while her henna is on her.'
Muhammad ibn al-Ḥasan said: This report is understood as indicating recommendation (istiḥbāb) rather than obligation (wujūb), and that which indicates this is what he narrated:

key_terms.اَلْوُجُوبُ: Obligation; a legal ruling where the act must be performed
key_terms.اِسْتِحْبَابٌ: Recommendation; a legal ruling where doing the act is rewarded but omitting it is not penalized
key_terms.خِضَابُ: Henna or dye applied to the body, specifically hands and feet
key_terms.يَنْزِعُهُ: To remove or take off (the henna)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray with henna on the hands or feet according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* addresses the fiqh of ritual purity regarding henna (khidhāb) on the skin during prayer. While the Imam initially indicates that one should not pray with henna on, the scholar Muhammad ibn al-Hasan clarifies that this is likely a recommendation (istiḥbāb) rather than a strict obligation (wujūb), provided the substance is clean. This ruling applies equally to men and women, reflecting the Shia juristic view that henna does not form an impermeable barrier preventing water from reaching the skin during ablution (wuḍū).
